questions.knowledge_point: Factoring a Sum of Squares
questions.worked_solution:
To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${i}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+36 & ={x}^{2}-(-36) \\  & ={x}^{2}-(36{i}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{2}-(6i)^{2} \\  & =(x+6i)(x-6i)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The expression $9p+p{t}^{2}$ is equivalent to
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's factor $p$ from the expression. We have

$$
9p+p{t}^{2}=p(9+{t}^{2}).
$$

Let's now focus on factoring the expression $(9+{t}^{2}).$

To factor a sum of squares, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${\text{i}}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}9+{t}^{2} & =9-(-{t}^{2}) \\  & =9-({\text{i}}^{2}{t}^{2}) \\  & ={3}^{2}-(\text{i}t)^{2} \\  & =(3+\text{i}t)(3-\text{i}t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
p(9+{t}^{2})=p(3+\text{i}t)(3-\text{i}t).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}81{y}^{4}+18{y}^{2}+1 & ={(9{y}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot (9{y}^{2})\cdot 1+{1}^{2} \\  & ={(9{y}^{2}+1)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to factor the sum of squares in the parentheses. To do this, we first write it as a difference. Then, we rewrite the second term using ${i}^{2}=-1.$ Finally, we factor as a difference of squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}9{y}^{2}+1 & =9{y}^{2}-(-1) \\  & =9{y}^{2}-({i}^{2}) \\  & ={(3y)}^{2}-{(i)}^{2} \\  & =(3y+i)(3y-i)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this back into our main expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}81{y}^{4}+18{y}^{2}+1 & ={(9{y}^{2}+1)}^{2} \\  & ={((3y+i)(3y-i))}^{2} \\  & ={(3y+i)}^{2}{(3y-i)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
